metadata.title: It Updates the Model. Not Itself.
metadata.subtitle: The Model-Update Skill (Financial Model Refresh)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when a Claude Skill called "model update" runs, does it update Claude itself, or a financial model? Lands the carry-out that a model update doesn't make Claude smarter — it makes the model current, and the decision still belongs to a person.

beats.narration_text: People hear "model update" and assume Claude itself just got smarter. It didn't. Liam here, in for Bear — let's take this skill apart. What actually updates when new numbers land is a spreadsheet, not Claude. So what's really running in there?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it lifts a finger. This one is called model-update. Open it and there's exactly one file inside — SKILL.md — written in plain English. No hidden branches, no compiled code. Claude reads the file, then does what it says. That's a design choice: the file is the whole program. Anyone can open it. Anyone can change it. Nothing is hiding behind a wrapper.

Inside SKILL.md the instructions are a numbered list, and Claude runs them top to bottom. Step one: take the new data in — an earnings print, revised guidance, a changed assumption. Step two: adjust the estimates and recalculate the valuation. Step three: flag whatever changed enough to matter. No branching, unless a step itself tells it to branch. That's the trade they picked — reproducibility over cleverness. Same list, same order, same result, every run.

This is why the skill exists — so nobody redoes the same update by hand every time new numbers land. Model-update takes what changed — quarterly earnings, new guidance, a revised assumption — and runs it through: new estimates, a recalculated valuation, a flag on anything material. And here's what it does not touch. Claude isn't updated. The weights, the training — untouched. What updates is the model, using data Claude is handed for that one run. Nothing carries over to the next. The investment call still belongs to a person: the skill flags what changed, it doesn't decide what to do about it. They optimized for a repeatable refresh at the expense of an automated call — the human is doing the judgment on purpose.
A model update doesn't make Claude smarter — it makes the model current, and the decision still belongs to a person.

props.quote: A model update doesn't make Claude smarter — it makes the model current, and the decision still belongs to a person.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Hand it your estimates — say, 8% revenue growth, a 22% operating margin, a DCF you already built — then throw new numbers at it: an earnings print that beat on revenue but missed on margin by 200 basis points, guidance cut from 8% growth to 6%, and capex stepping up 15%. Before it touches a cell, ask it to walk you through exactly which estimates it would adjust, how the valuation changes, and what it would flag as material — then wait for you to say go. That's the model-update loop, run by hand: update, flag, stop. Go deeper: ask it to name three sets of new numbers where the model still ties out cleanly and still hands a person the wrong call — and describe what the skill would need to do to catch each one.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to run the model-update loop by hand and see what it actually does. Pretend I own a valuation of a public company with these estimates: revenue growth of 8% next year, operating margin of 22%, and a discounted-cash-flow valuation I already built off those. New numbers just landed: an earnings print that beat on revenue but missed on operating margin by 200 basis points, revised guidance that lowers next year's growth from 8% to 6%, and a changed assumption that capex will step up by 15%. Before you touch a single cell, walk me through exactly which estimates you would adjust, how the valuation changes as a result, and which line items you would flag as material — then wait for me to say go. Do not decide the investment call. Just do the update, flag what matters, and stop.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: name three sets of new numbers where a model-update pass would tie out cleanly, look freshly updated, and still hand a person the wrong investment call — and for each one describe what the skill would need to do to catch it.
